To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Australian retirement income system is in need of reform.
the 2007 reforms have created a system that is no longer simply about income protection in retirement but also about wealth accumulation.
the current Australian retirement income arrangements are a hybrid system of public and private arrangements that are at variance with the intent and objectives of the earlier reforms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the following questions: What has been the evolution of the retirement income arrangements of Australia since the mid-1980s?
the question: What is the appropriate role of the state in the provision of retirement income?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the policy changes of 2007 are not a return to the policy slipperiness of the 1981 crossroad but rather a further step away from the policy coherence achieved in the 1980-1990s.
Australia is not yet at the end of a long and tortuous road.
the current arrangements are not the best that could have been devised, but that they are not the worst either.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have not yet reached the 'end of history' as far as retirement income policy is concerned.
the current arrangements are not only inconsistent with the original goals of superannuation but also with the intent of recent reforms.
we have a system that is no longer fit for purpose.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the current system has become too complex, and the policy goals of its constituent parts have become blurred, to the extent that the system no longer functions as intended.
